newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African gas-fired power stations not seen viable.
newsitem.headline: S.African gas-fired power stations not seen viable.

text.p: Gas-fired power stations are unlikely ever to be viable in South Africa, despite a double choice of large natural gas fields in neighbouring Mozambique and Namibia, industry officials said on Tuesday.

"Gas in South Africa has great difficulty in competing with coal which is available to (electricity generator) Eskom at extremely low prices," said Tony Way of Enron Corp, which is developing Mozambique's Pande gas field project.
"It is difficult to foresee when a time would come when gas would be able to compete with coal in gas-fired power generation."
Gas-fired power stations have been mooted on South Africa's east or west coast to utilise gas from Pande or Namibia's Kudu field.
Johan Fourie from the gas division of synthetic fuel producer Sasol Ltd, speaking at the Africa Oil conference with Way, agreed power generation from natural or coal-based gas was simply not viable.

Residential useage was also effectively ruled out for climatic reasons -- the short South african winter would not create enough demand -- and Way said the Pande field was too small to justify a liquefied natural gas (LNG) project.
Instead, the focus is on industrial applications, and here Way said developments were encouraging.
Initial investigations into the viability of establishing a South African iron ore reduction plant using Pande gas were going well, he said.

Two months ago Enron and Mozambique government's ENH hydrocarbon concern signed a heads of agreement with South Africa's state-run Industral Development Corp (IDC) on the potential export of gas to fuel an iron plant in northern South Africa.

Way said the first phase of the IDC's feasibiluty study on the the large-scale project would be completed by December, with the full study and funding plans due to be finished by end 1997. If all went according to plan, Pande would start pumping gas through a planned 900 km pipeline running via Maputo by 2000 at the rate of 150 million cubic feet a day, he said.
Gas had a competitive edge over coal is this area because it was a more efficient for iron ore reduction, he said.

In addition to the "anchor load" of the planned iron plant, Way said he was also hopeful an ammonia and urea facility would be started up in Maputo, using further gas from Pande which has reserves of 2.0-2.5 trillion cubic feet.
